head: Lunchboxes cross Mumbai
and rarely get lost.
slides.sub: How couriers with no computers built one of the world's most reliable delivery systems.

image.label: Rows of round metal lunchboxes stacked on a station platform
image.brief: 아침 뭄바이 기차역 플랫폼에 줄지어 쌓인 둥근 금속 도시락통들. 뚜껑에 손으로 칠한 색 표시. 흰 모자를 쓴 인물들은 뒷모습 실루엣으로만. 따뜻한 햇빛, 분주한 분위기.

head: Home-cooked lunch,
carried across a city.
body: In the 1890s, Mumbai was filling with office workers who had long commutes and no canteens. A story often told credits Mahadeo Havaji Bachche with starting a lunch delivery service for them.
The idea was simple: collect a hot meal from each home in the morning and have it on the worker's desk by lunchtime.

image.label: A colonial-era Bombay street with office workers and handcarts
image.brief: 19세기 말 봄베이 거리. 식민지 시대 석조 건물, 사무원들과 손수레. 세피아 톤. 실존 인물 얼굴 없음.

slides.label: lunchboxes delivered on a typical working day, by most estimates
body: Around 5,000 dabbawalas do the work, many from farming villages near Pune, and many with little formal schooling. They work in small groups and share in the earnings of the trust that organises them.

image.label: Hundreds of lunchboxes arranged in long wooden crates
image.brief: 긴 나무 상자에 빼곡히 담긴 수백 개의 금속 도시락통을 위에서 내려다본 구도. 규모감이 느껴지게.

head: About three hours.
No room for a slip.
body: Each box changes hands several times. One dabbawala collects it from a kitchen, sorters regroup it at a station, a train carries it downtown, and another dabbawala cycles it to the office.
Then the empty box makes the same trip home. Miss one train and a whole batch of lunches is late.

image.label: A courier on a bicycle loaded with lunchboxes in traffic
image.brief: 도시락통을 잔뜩 실은 자전거를 탄 배달원이 뭄바이 도로 교통 속을 달리는 모습. 뒷모습 또는 실루엣. 움직임이 느껴지는 흐린 배경.

head: Millions of handoffs.
How do you keep order?
body: Your workforce is large, many can't read long addresses, and there are no computers. Volume keeps growing every year.

options.text: Use a short painted code on every lid and a fixed relay tied to the train timetable
options.feedback: Cheap and easy to learn, but it only works if everyone sticks to the same rules every day. Keep swiping.

options.text: Set up a central dispatch office with supervisors tracking every box
options.feedback: More control, but every decision waits for the centre, and that adds cost and delay. Keep swiping.

options.text: Hire only literate couriers and write full addresses on each box
options.feedback: Clearer labels, but a smaller pool of workers and slower reading at every handoff. Keep swiping.

image.label: A busy sorting point at a railway station at mid-morning
image.brief: 오전 기차역의 분주한 분류 장소. 바닥에 놓인 도시락통 무리와 바쁘게 움직이는 손들. 얼굴은 보이지 않게.

head: No addresses.
Just a few marks.
body: The dabbawalas chose the code. Each lid carries a few painted colours, numbers and letters showing the pickup area, the arrival station, the building and the floor.
Anyone in the system can read it at a glance. New workers learn it quickly, and it has barely changed in decades.

image.label: Close-up of a lunchbox lid with painted coloured symbols
image.brief: 도시락 뚜껑 클로즈업. 손으로 칠한 색깔 점, 숫자, 알파벳 기호. 실제 코드를 정확히 재현하지 않은 일반적 디자인.

head: The train sets the pace.
Everyone keeps time.
body: Boxes are sorted by destination, loaded onto suburban trains in crates and split up again at the other end. Each small group covers its own patch and covers for absent members.
With a fixed timetable, the work moves like a relay, with no control room.

image.label: Crates of lunchboxes loaded into a suburban train carriage
image.brief: 뭄바이 교외 열차 칸에 실리는 도시락 상자들. 열린 문, 플랫폼의 시계. 인물은 실루엣.

head: How few errors?
Nobody counted exactly.
body: A claim often repeated says they make one mistake in 16 million deliveries. That figure never came from a formal audit.
What is well documented is the reputation: customers have trusted them for generations, and Harvard Business School wrote a case on how they work.

image.label: A lunchbox placed on an office desk at noon
image.brief: 정오의 사무실 책상 위에 놓인 도시락통 하나. 창으로 들어오는 햇빛. 사람은 손만 보이게.

head: Don't train out mistakes.
Design them out.
body: The dabbawalas didn't rely on technology or star employees. A simple code, a fixed schedule and small accountable teams made the right move the easy one.
Every step is standard, so any worker can handle any box, and an error shows up fast.

image.label: Simple flow diagram drawn over a railway map
image.brief: 철도 노선도 위에 겹쳐진 단순한 흐름도 그래픽. 화살표와 점으로 릴레이를 표현.

head: Simple systems
beat clever people.
body: Reliability comes from design, not heroics. Fewer choices at each handoff means fewer chances to slip.
**Try it today:** pick one handoff in your business where things go wrong. What one mark, rule or fixed time would make the right action obvious?

image.label: A single lunchbox on an empty platform at dusk
image.brief: 해 질 녘 텅 빈 기차역 플랫폼에 놓인 도시락통 하나. 차분하고 따뜻한 톤.

factChecks.note: 1890년 시작과 Mahadeo Havaji Bachche 창시설은 널리 전해지는 이야기입니다. 카드에는 "a story often told"로 표시했습니다. Nutan Mumbai Tiffin Box Suppliers Charity Trust 자료와 주요 언론 보도로 확인하세요.

하루 약 20만 개 도시락, 다바왈라 약 5,000명은 언론과 단체 측이 자주 인용하는 수치입니다. 자료마다 13만~20만 개, 4,500~5,000명으로 다르므로 "by most estimates", "around"로 적었습니다. 코로나 이후에는 크게 줄었다는 보도가 있으니 현재 시점 표현에 주의하세요. → [2026-11-02 확인] 1890년 시작, 약 5,000명, 하루 약 20만 건 확인.

"1,600만 건 중 1건 오류"와 "식스시그마 인증" 주장은 흔히 Forbes(1998) 보도로 전해지지만 공식 감사나 인증으로 확인된 수치가 아닙니다. 제안된 각도(오류가 거의 없다)를 그대로 단정하지 않고, 카드에서 확인되지 않은 수치임을 밝혔습니다. → [2026-11-02 확인] '1,600만 건 중 1건' 주장과 Forbes·식스시그마 인증은 단체 대표도 부인했다는 기록 확인. 카드의 '공식 감사 없음' 서술과 일치.
Harvard Business School 케이스(Stefan Thomke 등, 2012년 무렵 "Mumbai's Models of Service Excellence")가 있는지 제목과 연도를 확인하세요. 카드에는 학교 이름만 적었습니다.
도시락 뚜껑의 색·숫자·문자 코드가 출발 지역, 도착역, 건물, 층을 나타낸다는 설명은 여러 보도와 연구에 나옵니다. 코드 구성 요소는 자료마다 조금씩 다르니 확인하세요.
다바왈라 상당수가 푸네 인근 농촌 출신이고 정규 교육이 적다는 점, 소그룹 운영과 트러스트 구성원으로 수익을 나눈다는 점은 단체 설명과 보도 기준입니다.
